intro: Guided sequences through the collection. Each trail is a short argument made of passages; read them in order.

stops.note: A three-word command creates intimacy before the drifting starts.
Irony presented as a universal truth.
Antithesis stacked until one sentence holds a whole era's contradictions.
One wrong detail — clocks striking thirteen — signals a changed world.
The alliteration wins the ear before the meaning arrives.
One sentence holds three times at once: the firing squad, the memory, the ice.

trails.title: The rhetoric of protest
trails.blurb: Public speech under pressure, from declaration to refusal.

stops.note: A periodic sentence delays its main clause while the grievances pile up.
Antithesis and epistrophe compress a war into 272 words.
Balanced clauses refuse vengeance at the moment of victory.
Anaphora drives the speech: the dream clause returns until it sounds inevitable.
One long periodic sentence carries the whole meaning of "wait."
Rhetorical questions push back; the repeated refrain rises each time.

trails.title: Shakespeare's balance sheet
trails.blurb: Five speeches, five ways syntax carries a mind under strain.

stops.note: Conditionals and alternatives: logic applied to a problem logic can't solve.
Infinitives with no subject: the grammar itself can't act.
Repetition that goes nowhere, on purpose.
Lear shouts commands at the storm — apostrophe at full volume.
Identical sentence structures arguing identical humanity.

trails.title: Grief and consolation
trails.blurb: How form holds feeling that would otherwise overwhelm it.

stops.note: Death appears as a polite coachman; the dashes read as held breath.
The quatrain contains the grief so the speaker can go on.
Suffering sits in the corner of the canvas; the understatement does the damage.
The two refrains keep returning, and each return is a refusal.
Litotes repeated until it breaks: "the art of losing isn't hard to master."

trails.title: The sentence as performance
trails.blurb: Five writers pushing syntax past what prose is supposed to do.

stops.note: Proust uses the long sentence to hold memory.
Syntax stripped of hierarchy: perception without interpretation.
Polysyndeton without relief: and, and, and.
Fragments doing work that whole sentences won't.
A chorus of voices takes over; the sentence dissolves into testimony.

trails.title: First person, singular
trails.blurb: Six narrators whose grammar is their character.

stops.note: Digression becomes character — the voice can't stay on topic, and that's the portrait.
A paradox in the first breath: an invisible man, telling you so.
Direct address claims its authority outright: "Reader, I married him."
Flat parataxis: short sentences that refuse to show feeling.
Cumulative sentences, unhurried, in a father's voice.
Observation sharpened into aphorism.
